content: Carnauba wax is a natural wax obtained from the leaves of the carnauba palm tree, scientifically known as Copernicia prunifera, which is native to northeastern Brazil. It is often referred to as the queen of waxes due to its unique properties and is typically found in the form of hard, yellow-brown flakes. The wax is harvested by collecting the leaves of the carnauba palm, beating them to release the wax, and then refining and bleaching it to achieve the final product. Carnauba wax is primarily composed of esters of fatty acids, which make up 80-85% of its content. It also contains fatty alcohols (10-16%), free acids (3-6%), and hydrocarbons (1-3%). Notably, it includes esterified fatty diols (approximately 20%), hydroxylated fatty acids (around 6%), and cinnamic acid (about 10%). Cinnamic acid, which is known for its antioxidant properties, may exist in hydroxylated or methoxylated forms. Carnauba wax is widely used for its ability to produce a glossy finish. It is a key ingredient in automobile waxes, shoe polishes, and polishes for instruments, floors, and furniture, especially when combined with beeswax. It is also used as a coating for dental floss and is the most common material for paper coatings in the United States. In the surfboard industry, it is the primary component of surfboard wax, often mixed with coconut oil. In the cosmetics industry, carnauba wax is a prominent ingredient in products such as lipsticks, eyeliners, mascaras, eye shadows, foundations, blushers, and various skin and sun care preparations. It is also the preferred finish for briar pipes, as it produces a high-gloss finish when buffed onto wood. Over time, this finish dulls rather than flaking off, which is a common issue with other finishes. In the food industry, carnauba wax serves multiple purposes, including as a formulation aid, lubricant, release agent, anticaking agent, and surface finishing agent. It is used in baked goods, chewing gum, confections, frostings, fresh fruits and juices, gravies, sauces, processed fruits and juices, soft candies, and products like Tic Tacs and Altoids. In the pharmaceutical industry, it is employed as a coating agent for tablets. Historically, in 1890, Charles Tainter patented the use of carnauba wax on phonograph cylinders as a replacement for a paraffin and beeswax mixture. When used as a mold release agent, carnauba wax is particularly advantageous because, unlike silicone or PTFE, it is compatible with liquid epoxy, epoxy molding compounds (EMC), and certain other plastics. It enhances the properties of epoxies and most engineering plastics. An aerosol mold release can be created by suspending carnauba wax in a solvent, which is widely used in molds for semiconductor devices. Additionally, semiconductor manufacturers use chunks of carnauba wax to break in new epoxy molds or to release stuck plungers. From a technical perspective, the International Nomenclature of Cosmetic Ingredients (INCI) name for carnauba wax is Copernicia Cerifera (carnauba) wax, and its E number is E903. It has a melting point of 78-85°C, which is among the highest of all natural waxes. Its relative density is approximately 0.97. Carnauba wax is one of the hardest natural waxes, even harder than concrete in its pure form. It is practically insoluble in water but can dissolve when heated in ethyl acetate or xylene. It is, however, practically insoluble in ethyl alcohol.
